source_text: Cui aspectui quoniam multum sunt inimica phantasmata, quae de carnali sensu tracta imaginarie cogitatio nostra uersat et continet, detestemur istam haeresim, quae suorum phantasmatum fidem secuta et diuinam substantiam per locorum spatia quamuis infinita uelut informem molem disiecit atque diffudit et eam ex una parte truncauit, ut inueniret locum malo, quod uidere non potuit non esse naturam, sed contra naturam, et ipsum malum tanta specie et formis et pace partium in singulis naturis uigente decorauit, quia sine his bonis nullam poterat cogitare naturam, ut ea mala, quae ibi reprehendit, innumerabilium bonorum copia sepeliantur. sed huius uoluminis iste sit terminus; in ceteris cetera eius deliramenta deo permittente atque adiuuante arguentur.
thought_title: Against the fantasies that deform God
orientation: Augustine is closing the treatise by urging rejection of Mani's heresy because its fantasies about God as a bodily mass led it to invent a place for evil.
pass_a_gloss: Since fantasies are very hostile to that sight, which drawn from carnal sense our imaginative thought turns over and holds, let us detest this heresy, which followed faith in its own fantasies and scattered and poured out the divine substance through the spaces of places, although infinite, as if a shapeless mass, and cut it off from one part, so that it might find a place for evil, which it could not see to be not a nature, but against nature, and it adorned that very evil with so great form and forms and peace of parts thriving in individual natures, because without these goods it could think no nature, so that those evils, which it reproaches there, are buried by the abundance of innumerable goods. But let this be the end of this volume; in the rest, its other ravings will be refuted, with God permitting and helping.

choices.why: Glossary term for images formed from bodily sense experience; Augustine uses it here for the mental images that misrepresent God.
Glossary term 'substance' for underlying reality; 'divine substance' renders the phrase literally and keeps the theological force.
Literal rendering of 'informem' as 'shapeless' and 'molem' as 'mass' to convey Mani's bodily conception of God.

choices.term: non esse naturam, sed contra naturam
choices.english: not to be a nature, but against nature
choices.why: Keeps the exact antithesis and the glossary term 'nature'; the clause is central to Augustine's argument that evil is not a substance.
rejected: not a nature but contrary to nature
not a substance but against nature

choices.term: specie et formis et pace partium
choices.english: form and forms and peace of parts
choices.why: Literal rendering of the three goods Augustine names; 'species' is glossary 'form', and 'formis' is plural 'forms'.
rejected: beauty and shapes and harmony of parts

choices.why: Literal and dismissive, matching Augustine's polemical tone against Mani's teachings.

pass_b_english: Since fantasies are great enemies of that sight—fantasies which our thought, drawn from carnal sense, turns over and holds in the imagination—let us detest this heresy. It followed the credence of its own fantasies, and it scattered and spread the divine substance through the expanses of places, however infinite, as if it were a shapeless mass, and cut it off on one side so that it could find a place for evil. which it could not see was not a nature, but against nature. And it adorned that very evil with such form and forms and peace of parts thriving in each nature—because without these goods it could not think of any nature—so that the evils it finds fault with there are buried under a wealth of countless goods. But let this be the end of this book; in the remaining ones, with God permitting and helping, the rest of its ravings will be refuted.

problems.quote: as if it were a shapeless mass, however infinite
problems.source_quote: uelut informem molem disiecit atque diffudit
problems.why: Latin 'uelut informem molem' modifies the divine substance as 'like a shapeless mass'; 'however infinite' (quamuis infinita) modifies 'expanses of places,' not the mass. The syntax is misread.
problems.fix: through expanses of places, however infinite, as if it were a shapeless mass
problems.ruling: 'quamuis infinita' agrees with 'spatia locorum' (neuter plural), not 'molem' (feminine); misattached to mass.

problems.quote: It could not see that evil is not a nature, but against nature
problems.source_quote: quod uidere non potuit non esse naturam, sed contra naturam
problems.why: The subject of 'uidere non potuit' is the heresy, but the antecedent of 'quod' is 'malum'—'evil which it could not see was not a nature.' The English makes a new clause with unclear subject.
problems.fix: evil which it could not see was not a nature, but against nature
problems.ruling: 'quod' is relative pronoun with 'malo' as antecedent; English 'It could not see that...' misreads syntax and subject.

edits.new: through the expanses of places, however infinite, as if it were a shapeless mass

fixed: Reordered 'however infinite' to modify 'expanses of places' as in the source 'per locorum spatia quamuis infinita uelut informem molem'.
Changed 'is not' to 'was not' to reflect the source's indirect statement 'non esse naturam, sed contra naturam' dependent on 'uidere non potuit'.

problems.quote: It followed faith in its own fantasies
problems.why: Latin 'fidem secuta' means 'following the faith/belief of its own fantasies,' not 'followed faith in its own fantasies.' The heresy followed/trusted its fantasies as a guide.
problems.fix: which followed the credence of its own fantasies

problems.quote: It could not see that evil was not a nature, but against nature
problems.source_quote: quod uidere non potuit non esse naturam, sed contra naturam
problems.why: The subject is wrong: not 'It could not see' but 'which [evil] it could not see was not a nature.' The heresy failed to perceive that evil itself is not a nature.
problems.fix: which it could not see was not a nature, but against nature
problems.ruling: 'quod' is accusative subject of 'non esse naturam': evil which it could not see to be non-nature. English misreads syntax.

fixed: Changed 'It followed faith in its own fantasies' to 'It followed the credence of its own fantasies' to reflect 'fidem secuta' as following the belief/credence of its fantasies.

Changed 'It could not see that evil was not a nature, but against nature.' to 'which it could not see was not a nature, but against nature.' to make 'evil' the object of perception, matching 'quod uidere non potuit non esse naturam.'

sweep.held_why: 1 confirmed problems after 2 repairs; repair made no edit

dismissed.quote: which it could not see was not a nature, but against nature
dismissed.why: Missing 'non' before 'uidere': 'could not see' should be 'could not see that it was not a nature'—the Latin says Mani failed to see evil was NOT a nature, but the English makes it sound like he failed to see it WAS a nature.
dismissed.note: The quoted wording renders the Latin correctly, and the proposed fix is the same text; a separate problem sits just outside the quote: the stray period in 'a place for evil. which' makes a sentence fragment and should be a comma.
